episode.title: Cariboo Signals - Repair Culture & Practical Tech
episode.description:
Riley and Casey explore technology and society in rural communities. Today's focus: Repair Culture & Practical Tech.

THIS WEEK WE'RE ASKING: When is small genuinely better, and when is it just an excuse?

NEWS ROUNDUP: We break down Emergency officials called to motel in 100 Mile House and Flames destroy house on Horsefly Road near Williams Lake, plus 11 more stories, and explore what these developments mean for communities like ours.

RURAL CONNECTIONS: Is a household running its own encryption and digital security really self-reliance, or is it just unpaid labor that someone has shifted onto individuals? Topics include: Cost versus skill gap in household digital security adoption, Repairability and right-to-repair as design ethics in consumer electronics, Large institutional security failures versus small-scale household setups and visibility as a risk factor, Knowledge preservation and documentation in small rural communities and repair shops, Testing and verification of backup and recovery systems before emergencies occur.

Hosts: Riley (Tech optimist with an engineering background) and Casey (Community-first skeptic of tech promises).

COMMUNITY SPOTLIGHT: Cariboo Regional District Library

discussion.central_question: Is a household running its own encryption and digital security really self-reliance, or is it just unpaid labor that someone has shifted onto individuals?
discussion.riley_position: The tools for household digital security are now free and accessible, making self-reliance genuinely possible; the problem is a skill gap rather than a cost barrier, and small-scale setups may actually be safer than large institutions since they're less visible targets and don't accumulate massive data pools.
riley_key_evidence: TechRadar story of a 220 million traveler record breach from a misconfigured provider system showing that institutions with dedicated security teams fail at scale
AirPods 5 teardown showing Apple finally broke a decade of zero repairability scores, proving that pressure on design practices creates measurable change
ShinyHunters hacking into Cl0p ransomware gang demonstrates that criminal operations attack each other, meaning the threat landscape is fragmented rather than monolithic
discussion.casey_position: Free tools don't solve the actual problem of ongoing maintenance and knowledge preservation; rural households often lack anyone who understands encryption at all, and when the one person who set up a system leaves, the knowledge vanishes, creating a hidden countdown clock that nobody's watching.
casey_key_evidence: No NDP or Green candidates had filed yet in either Cariboo riding as of the reporting date, showing election readiness varies by party
Rural communities like Wells have no local IT support infrastructure, so relying on one knowledgeable person creates a single point of failure
The airline breach involved nine years of passport data despite dedicated IT staff, proving that scale doesn't guarantee competence and that institutions also fail at basic security hygiene
discussion.resolution: Riley and Casey agreed that the actual failure point isn't household versus institution—it's whether anyone tests the recovery process before an emergency happens, a testable claim that applies equally to both. They proposed the library could hold sealed copies of recovery instructions, and invited listeners to conduct their own restore tests and report the results.
topics_covered: Cost versus skill gap in household digital security adoption
Repairability and right-to-repair as design ethics in consumer electronics
Large institutional security failures versus small-scale household setups and visibility as a risk factor
Knowledge preservation and documentation in small rural communities and repair shops
Testing and verification of backup and recovery systems before emergencies occur
calls_to_action: Write down recovery keys somewhere durable and document the encryption setup so a second person could follow it without calling the original builder—then try having someone else restore from the backup without assistance as a real test.
The Cariboo Regional District Library could potentially hold sealed copies of household recovery key instructions, functioning as a digital fire safe for encryption documentation.

If you have a story about how your digital security setup handles recovery testing, send it to feedback at cariboosignals.ca—listeners are invited to conduct their own restore tests and report the actual results to the show.

This is enough. I'll compile final findings.

PRE-RESEARCHED INSIGHTS FOR THE DEEP DIVE

RESEARCH QUESTION: Who has filed/been nominated for the 2026 B.C. election in Cariboo-Chilcotin, and what is their record?
Findings: Lorne Doerkson (Conservative Party) has filed with Elections BC as "MLA before dissolution" for Cariboo-Chilcotin (BC Ballot, bcballot.ca/candidates/, accessed 2026). He first won the riding in 2020 as a B.C. Liberal with 6,600 votes (51.25%), a margin of roughly 19 points over NDP's Scott Andrews at 4,180 votes/32.46% (Elections BC statement of votes, 2020 general election PDF). He was re-elected in 2024 as a B.C. Conservative by a margin of 7,722 votes (BC Ballot, bcballot.ca, 2026). Doerkson was named interim leader of the B.C. Conservative Party by the party board following Kerry-Lynne Findlay's resignation on Sept. 21, 2026, after what the Chilliwack Progress (Sept. 23, 2026) called Findlay's "scandal-plagued tenure of under four months in which the party nearly split in two." CBC News (2026) reported the "Cariboo-Chilcotin MLA takes over a party in turmoil amid speculation of" an early election call. No NDP, Green, or other party candidate for Cariboo-Chilcotin in 2026 has been established by this search.
Suggested angle: Riley could frame Doerkson's rise from a low-profile riding MLA to party leader amid caucus chaos as evidence that rural B.C. politics still produces stabilizing figures; Casey could push back that a leader installed by "party board" appointment rather than a membership vote, amid a near-split party, raises questions about legitimacy the show should flag as a finding, not settled fact, going into the Oct. 24, 2026 vote.

RESEARCH QUESTION: Who has filed/been nominated for the 2026 B.C. election in Prince George-North Cariboo, and what is Sheldon Clare's record?
Findings: The Prince George Citizen (2026) reported Sheldon Clare "is on the ballot in Prince George-North Cariboo" for the B.C. Conservatives in 2026. Clare first won the riding in 2024 with 56.82% of the vote (11,430 votes per Wikipedia's cited Elections BC figures; other outlets reported slightly different counts during the count night — My Prince George Now reported 10,849/56.76% and Prince George Citizen reported 10,481/56.5% on election night before final counts, 2024-10-19), unseating BC United incumbent Coralee Oakes, who ran as an independent and placed second with 21.84% (a margin of roughly 35 points, per Wikipedia's electoral history table sourced to Elections BC). NDP's Denice Bardua placed third with 17.03% and Green's Randy Thompson was fourth with 4.31% in that 2024 race. Clare briefly ran for the B.C. Conservative Party leadership in January 2026 (Victoria Times Colonist / CTV News, Jan. 8, 2026) but withdrew alongside Richmond-Queensborough MLA Steve Kooner on Feb. 27, 2026 (Williams Lake Tribune, Victoria News, Keremeos Review, CFJC Today, Feb. 27–28, 2026). The leadership contest was won by Kerry-Lynne Findlay on May 30, 2026 with 51% of points in a fourth-round count over Caroline Elliott's 49% (Wikipedia, "2026 Conservative Party of British Columbia leadership election"). Clare became the Opposition House Leader on June 29, 2026 (Wikipedia). No NDP or Green candidate for Prince George-North Cariboo in 2026 has been established by this search; a search result notes Randy Thompson was the 2024 Green candidate, not confirmed for 2026.
Suggested angle: Casey could question why a sitting MLA's leadership ambitions (Clare's brief run, then withdrawal) get less local coverage than the horse-race outcome, and press on whether that reflects genuine local priorities or party-level distraction reaching into the riding; Riley could counter that Clare's return to a House Leader role post-withdrawal shows the caucus still trusts him, a fact worth noting distinctly from the leadership contest's allegations of "funny business" that Clare himself addressed (Victoria Times Colonist/Canadian Press, Jan. 17, 2026, where Clare said leadership rules were meant to stop "funny business").

NO RECORD FOUND: any NDP candidate for Cariboo-Chilcotin 2026; any NDP or Green candidate for Prince George-North Cariboo 2026
